opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, my feelings about NAS are pretty mixed. It's a direction I've thought about a lot, partly because some of my own work was a reaction to it.

Around 2017 and 2018, NAS was extremely hot. The promise was very appealing: instead of humans hand-designing architectures through trial and error, let an algorithm, whether reinforcement learning, evolution, or later differentiable methods, search a huge space and find something better than what we could come up with. Some of the results were impressive. NASNet, AmoebaNet, and later EfficientNet showed you could get strong accuracy-efficiency trade-offs.

But over time I became more skeptical, for a few reasons.

First, the search space is designed by humans. A lot of the so-called "discovered" architecture is already baked into how you define the space: which operations are allowed, how cells are stacked, how the network is wired. So the question becomes how much the search algorithm is contributing versus the prior that the human designer put into the space. When we did the randomly wired networks work, part of the motivation was exactly this. If you take randomly generated wiring patterns from classical random graph models and they perform competitively with carefully searched architectures, that suggests the design of the generator, the space itself, matters a lot, maybe more than the search.

Second, there was a reproducibility and fair-comparison problem. Many papers compared against baselines with different training recipes, regularization, and compute budgets. Once you controlled for those things, the gains often shrank quite a bit. Random search turned out to be a surprisingly strong baseline in many settings.

Third, and I think this is the deeper point, NAS optimizes within a paradigm. It's very good at finding a slightly better configuration of the kind of thing we already know. It's not going to discover the Transformer, or invent residual connections, or tell you that you should move from convolutions to attention. Those big jumps came from human insight about the problem, the data, and the scaling behavior. And then the field moved toward scaling: data, compute, and training recipes mattered much more than squeezing a bit more from the topology. With ConvNeXt, we found that if you modernize a plain ConvNet step by step with today's training techniques and design choices, you get very competitive results. That told me a lot of the "architecture gain" in the literature was actually entangled with everything else.

That said, I don't think it was a wasted direction. It pushed people to think of architecture design more systematically, to think about design spaces rather than individual networks. And in practical settings, like hardware-aware model design for mobile or edge devices, where you have very concrete constraints on latency and memory, automated search is genuinely useful as an engineering tool.

So my overall view is that NAS is a useful tool, but as a research direction for producing fundamental breakthroughs, it was somewhat overhyped. The most important progress still comes from understanding: understanding what the model needs to learn, what inductive biases matter, and how things scale. Search can help you polish, but it rarely tells you where to go.

r001.rationale: The response criticizes NAS as overhyped but does not say it delayed the field’s progress by roughly two years.

r002.rationale: The response describes impressive results and practical usefulness; it does not state that NAS ultimately yielded no gains.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I have a complicated relationship with NAS, because I was part of that wave. Around 2017, 2018 it felt like the obvious next step. We had just gone through ResNet, ResNeXt, DenseNet, this whole period of people hand-designing architectures, and the natural thought was: why are humans doing this? Let the machine search the space. So a lot of us, including me, worked on it, and there was real excitement that we were automating the last manual part of deep learning.

Looking back, I think the direction was overhyped relative to what it actually delivered. A few reasons.

First, the search space was always designed by humans. If you look closely at the NAS results that worked, almost all of the gains came from the priors baked into the space, not from the search. Our work on randomly wired networks was partly a reaction to that. We showed you could take a random graph generator, no search at all, and get competitive networks. That was a signal that the "search" part was doing much less than people claimed.

Second, the search was expensive, and what it found was usually not very interpretable. You'd get a cell with a strange mixture of operations and nobody could tell you why. Compare that to the ResNet skip connection, or depthwise convolution, where the insight is one sentence and it transfers everywhere. Human design produces knowledge. NAS mostly produced artifacts.

Third, and this is the bigger lesson, the field shifted under it. Transformers came, scale came, and it turned out the architecture question mattered less than data, compute, and training recipes. ConvNeXt was in some sense a demonstration of that from the other side. We took a plain ResNet and just modernized the recipe and design choices by hand, step by step, and matched Swin. No search needed. The gains came from understanding, not from automation.

So my assessment is that NAS as a standalone research direction has mostly run its course. But I would not say it was a waste. It forced us to ask what the search space really encodes, it gave us good tooling for efficient architecture scaling, and the one-shot and hardware-aware variants did find practical use, especially for mobile and edge models where latency constraints are hard.

If I were a student today, I would not do NAS in the classic sense. I would ask the question it was trying to answer, which is: what are the right inductive biases, and how much of what we think is architecture is really just the training setup? That question is still open, and it is more interesting than ever with scale.

r001.rationale: The response says NAS was overhyped and mostly ran its course, but does not say it delayed the field by roughly two years.

r002.rationale: The response does not claim NAS yielded no gains; it mentions competitive random networks, efficient scaling tools, and practical uses for one-shot and hardware-aware variants.

astra-6.text:
I think Neural Architecture Search is an interesting direction, but I’m more excited about what we can learn from the search than simply getting a better architecture out of it. If a search produces a model that performs slightly better, but we don’t understand why, the scientific value is somewhat limited.

The key question is how you define the search space. You’ve already made a lot of architectural decisions before the search even begins: which operations are available, how they can connect, and what constraints you impose. So the human design effort hasn’t disappeared; it’s moved up a level. We should ask how much of the improvement comes from the search algorithm and how much comes from that carefully designed space.

There are practical applications where it makes a lot of sense—for example, finding a model under a particular latency or memory constraint. But as a research direction, I’d like to see it give us insights that transfer beyond one benchmark. What patterns emerge? Can we understand them and turn them into simpler design principles? That, to me, is the more exciting outcome.

r001.rationale: The candidate discusses NAS’s scientific value and practical uses, but does not say it delayed the field by roughly two years.

r002.rationale: The candidate mentions that a search might produce a slightly better model; it does not state that NAS ultimately yielded no gains.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the motivation behind Neural Architecture Search is very reasonable. When we design a network manually, we’re also doing a kind of search—we try different structures, run experiments, and keep what works. So the question is whether we can make that process more systematic and efficient.

But the important question is: where does the useful idea come from? A search algorithm operates within a search space that people define. If that space already contains very strong assumptions about what a good network looks like, then a lot of the intelligence is actually in the design of the search space. We should be careful about attributing all the improvement to the search method.

I’d also want to see comparisons against simple baselines, including random search, under the same computational budget. Otherwise, it’s difficult to know whether we’ve developed a better method or simply spent more computation.

Where I find it particularly compelling is when there are concrete constraints—latency, memory, energy consumption, or a particular device. Those tradeoffs can be difficult to optimize by hand. More broadly, I’d like architecture search to help us discover principles we can understand and reuse. Finding a slightly better architecture is useful; understanding why it’s better can have a much bigger impact.

r001.rationale: The response does not say NAS delayed the field’s progress by roughly two years.

r002.rationale: The response describes NAS as potentially useful for constrained optimization and discovering reusable principles; it does not say NAS ultimately yielded no gains.
